title: Hungary's New Leader Wants to Kick Out the President—by Changing the Rules!
summary: What do you do if you're the new boss of a country but the president won't leave? In Hungary, Prime Minister Péter Magyar is trying something big: he wants to change the constitution to remove President Tamás Sulyok. Magyar and his Tisza party won a huge election in April. They have enough votes in parliament to change laws. Magyar says Sulyok was appointed by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who led Hungary for 16 years. He calls Sulyok 'Orbán's puppet' and gave him until May 31 to resign. But on Monday, after a meeting at the presidential palace, Sulyok said no. So Magyar announced he would start the process to remove him, which could take about a month. The president's job in Hungary is mostly ceremonial—he signs laws and can send them to a court for review. Magyar's supporters worry Sulyok could block their plans. Magyar says the constitution says the president should 'guard the democratic functioning of the state,' and he thinks Sulyok failed by not speaking out against Orbán's actions, like banning LGBTQ+ Pride events. Orbán's party says removing a president this way is wrong and misuses power. Sulyok has asked European legal experts for advice. It's a big power struggle—and the whole country is watching.
why_it_matters: This fight shows that even in a democracy, the rules for who gets to lead can be changed—and that can affect whether all citizens, including minorities, are treated fairly.

background_read: Hungary is a country in Central Europe that used to be part of the Soviet bloc and is now a member of the European Union.
Viktor Orbán (Hungary’s prime minister from 2010 to 2025) was known for limiting LGBTQ+ rights and controlling much of the media, and he appointed Tamás Sulyok as president.
In many democracies, a president’s role is mostly ceremonial, so trying to change the constitution to remove one is a very unusual and major power move.
Article_Structure: WHO: Péter Magyar, the new Hungarian prime minister, and President Tamás Sulyok.
WHAT: Magyar wants to amend the constitution to force President Sulyok out after Sulyok refused to resign.
WHERE: The political struggle is unfolding in Hungary’s capital, Budapest, and its parliament.
WHY: Magyar believes Sulyok is a loyal follower of former leader Orbán and could block reforms, including those defending democratic values.

perspectives.description: His supporters argue that removing a president who does not speak up for democracy is necessary to protect equal rights after years of Orbán’s rule.
Orbán’s party warns that using the constitution to fire a president is a dangerous misuse of power and could become a political weapon.
The president has asked European legal experts for advice, signaling that whichever side wins, this struggle will test whether Hungary follows democratic norms.
